How does the US "democracy" work? I thought that as long as candidate gathers enough signatures to qualify for the election, he can participate in it. Obviously Trump is popular enough to do that. What is this shit about delegates, being nominated by party, or similar shit?

Not sure if you were expecting a real answer or being sarcastic but here you go:

The parties have their own system for picking their nominees - keep in mind this how the party is constructed and not necessarily US law. Of course if you want to run outside of one of the established parties - good luck. Washington had some choice words on political parties as he saw them emerge.

http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2014/dec/31/george-washingtons-views-political-parties-america/?page=all

In general, most primaries are decided within the first few weeks of states voting. This means that a handful of states out of the entire US pick the final candidate for each party most election cycles. Naturally everyone doesn't vote at once - they spread it out over months. The problem is that candidates typically drop out after results from only a few states (campaigns are expensive as fuck...).

Primary process is different for each state - some do straight voting, other do caucusing where you will actually meet and discuss politics with people from your own neighborhood. Most don't participant at this level. It is entirely possible for a candidate to be on the primary ballot in some states and not others (I think Ron Paul saw this problem a few years ago). In some states you have to be a declared party member to even participate (independents cannot vote for rep/dems) - in other states it doesn't matter if you are declared or not. In some states delegates are awarded proportionally - in some states it is winner take all.

In any case we barely saw 50% turnout in the last presidential election - even fewer people participate at the earlier primary levels to pick who the finalists will be.

http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2015/05/06/u-s-voter-turnout-trails-most-developed-countries/

US democracy works by giving people a choice between two parties that implement policy from the same political spectrum. This gives the illusion of choice even though policy is always the same (over reaching authoritarian government):

https://www.politicalcompass.org/uselection2016

Then you have 6 different media companies report on all main election information in the country. Really drive a rift around minimal party differences that will never change (abortion) to keep common people from uniting.

http://www.businessinsider.com/these-6-corporations-control-90-of-the-media-in-america-2012-6

And of course you allow those companies to make donations to the candidates they write about:

https://www.opensecrets.org/news/2010/08/news-corps-million-dollar-donation/

The result is most of the few people who do turn out to vote are not informed. If you don't have an informed electorate you cannot have a functioning democracy.
